newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK bankers in keen competition for H-share deals.
newsitem.headline: HK bankers in keen competition for H-share deals.

text.p: Sponsoring an H-share issue is less profitable and more risky than other IPOs, but merchant bankers are fiercely competing for the business in the hope it will lead to more China deals, corporate finance sources said.
"It will enable them to show a presence in the China market," Mark Chan, senior manager of capital markets at Nikko Securities Co (Asia), said on Thursday.
"It will also enhance their exposure in the high profile (international) market because H-share flotations always involve overseas placement," he added.

H-shares are stocks of Chinese state-owned enterprises listed in Hong Kong. Since the beginning of 1997, five Chinese enterprises have launched initial public offerings (IPO) in Hong Kong, taking advantage of investor interest in China-related stocks in the run-up to Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule.
Britain hands the territory back to China at midnight on June 30.
"Competition is always there and it is becoming more intensive," said Patrick Cheng, corporate finance director of HSBC Investment Banking.

Corporate finance executives said not only did merchant banks have to compete with local bankers for H-share deals, but had to contend with overseas players who were also keen to enter the China market.
"Unlike local issues (which are generally small in size), we have to face competition from all over the world," said Manus Tam, corporate finance director of Lippo Securities.
Winning the business was considered a type of "intangible asset", allowing a merchant bank to build a network for future business on the mainland, one corporate finance executive said.
Listing candidates usually pay a package fee that includes documentation and commission fees, corporate finance sources said.
Documentation fees vary from bank to bank, and can range from hundreds of thousands of dollars to a couple of million depending on the size of the issue, they said.
The commission fee is generally fixed at 2.5 percent of the value of the issue size.
"Some banks are reducing their fees in order to secure a sponsorship," said one corporate finance source.
While merchant bankers may be paid less for working on the deals, they may spend more time getting the issue to market.
Any delay in the listing process can be pricey since sponsors may need to re-prepare the listing document, especially since the accounting statement is normally valid for about six months.
"A bank may spend a year preparing an H-share issue but in return its income may be equal to its doing sponsorship for three smaller local issues in the same period of time," Tam said.
Merchant bankers said they may also be taking on more risk.
"The risk factors include judgement and quality -- whether it is a time consuming and cost effective issue, and how it will be received by investors," said HSBC Investment's Cheng.
"Short term atmosphere (in the IPO market in the next three months) is still positive and their (merchant banks) interest in sponsoring the (H-shares) issues are still keen," Tam added.

Zhejiang Expressway Co Ltd is the latest Chinese state-owned enterprise to list H-shares in Hong Kong. The stock made its trading debut on Thursday and closed at HK$2.50 compared with an issue price of HK$2.38.
